question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y={e}^{7+3x}$ as the composite function

$$
y={e}^{u},\,u=7+3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot 3 \\  & =3{e}^{u} \\  & =3{e}^{7+3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the sum rule of differentiation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}+{e}^{7+3x}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}+(3{e}^{7+3x}) \\  & =3({x}^{2}+{e}^{7+3x}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=-5{e}^{-3x}$ at the point where $x=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=-5{e}^{u},\,u=-3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-5{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-5{e}^{u}\cdot (-3) \\  & =15{e}^{u} \\  & =15{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$, evaluate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}m &= 15{e}^{-3x}\big|_{x=0} \\ &= 15{e}^{(-3)(0)} \\ &= 15.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}y_1 &= -5{e}^{-3x}\big|_{x=0} \\ &= -5{e}^{(-3)(0)} \\ &= -5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1 &=m(x-x_1) \\ y-(-5) &= (15)(x-(0)) \\ y-(-5) &= 15 x-(0) \\ y &= 15 x - 5.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=5{e}^{4x}$ at the point where $x=\frac{1}{4}.$

First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=5{e}^{u},\,u=4x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=5{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =5{e}^{u}\cdot 4 \\  & =20{e}^{u} \\  & =20{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{1}{4}$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=1/4} & ={(20{e}^{4x})|}_{x=1/4} \\  & =20{e}^{4(1/4)} \\  & =20e\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x={x}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & ={(5{e}^{4x})|}_{x=1/4} \\  & =5{e}^{4(1/4)} \\  & =5e.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-5e & =20e(x-\frac{1}{4}) \\ y-5e & =20ex-5e \\ y & =20ex\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)+6 e^{- 3 x}=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=1- 6 e^{- 3 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(1- 6 e^{- 3 x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=1\int 1\,\mathrm{d}x-6\int e^{- 3 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=1\left(x\right)-6\left(- \frac{e^{- 3 x}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=x + 2 e^{- 3 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Solve the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+e^{- 3 x}=6 x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} &=- e^{- 3 x}+6 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(- e^{- 3 x}+6 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ y &=-1\int e^{- 3 x}\,\mathrm{d}x+6\int x\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-1\left(- \frac{e^{- 3 x}}{3}\right)+6\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=3 x^{2} + \frac{e^{- 3 x}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)=\frac{2}{x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=\frac{2}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(\frac{2}{x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-6\int - \frac{1}{3 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-6\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(3 \left|{x}\right| \right)}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=2 \ln{\left(3 \left|{x}\right| \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

This solution holds on any interval that does not contain $x=0$.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/edb-math/repairs/2026-10-27-topic-audit-2/group-3/generator-assets/17592186087840/api/d9c29c262159309582f3c5ddcfa9935ef500eb10f5824171ce36dc90b3d18574.png)

What is the equation of the ellipse given above?

{{field-1}}$=1$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the horizontal radius has length $a=4$ and the vertical radius has length $b=\frac{17}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{\left(\frac{17}{2}\right)}^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{\left(\frac{289}{4}\right)} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{4{y}^{2}}{289} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Determining the Lengths of the Major and Minor Axes Given the Equation of an Ellipse

question.:question/problem:
For the ellipse $\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{81}=1,$ find the lengths of its major and minor axes.

$\,$ The length of the major axis is 
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ The length of the minor axis is 
{{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have ${a}^{2}=16$ and ${b}^{2}=81.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=16,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{16}=4.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=81,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{81}=9.$

Thus, the semi-major axis has length $b=9,$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=4.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 9=18,$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot 4=8.$

knowledge_point.title: Modeling Inhibited Growth

question.:question/problem: The growth of the number of animals in a rehabilitation aquarium is directly proportional to the difference between its maximum capacity and its current population. Let $M(t)$ be the number of animals, and let $t\ge 0$ be the time in months. If the maximum capacity is $85$ animals, which differential equation models this population? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change is proportional to the difference between the maximum capacity and the current quantity. Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=k(a-M),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum capacity and $k>0$.

Here $a=85$, so

$$
\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=k(85-M).
$$

domains.capacity: positive integer; current stock below capacity

question.:question/problem: A protected forest initially contains $106$ deer, and its maximum capacity is $249$ deer. Let $N(t)$ be the number of deer, where $t\ge 0$ is the time in years. Its population obeys an inhibited growth model. The rate of increase equals $\frac{3}{5}$ times the difference between the maximum capacity and the current population. Which differential equation models this population?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The rate at which the number of deer $N(t)$ in the protected forest changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum capacity and the current number of deer. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}=k(a-N),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum capacity, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=249$ deer, and $k=\frac{3}{5}$. Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{5}(249-N).
$$

question.:question/problem: The rate at which a liquid cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let $T(t)$ be the temperature of the liquid in degrees Celsius, and let $t>0$ be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is ${24}^{∘}\text{C},$ which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the liquid? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Write the equation in terms of the given constant $k$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={24}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-24).
$$

question.:question/problem:
A thermometer is placed into a water bath and displays a reading of ${78}^{∘}C.$ The thermometer is then transferred to a ${12}^{∘}C$ water bath, and its reading begins to decrease. After $12$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${58}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the thermometer to register a reading of ${28}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the thermometer decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the thermometer was transferred into the ${12}^{∘}C$ water bath.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={12}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-12).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-12| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-12>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-12 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-12 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-12 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =12+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${78}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=78,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}78 & =12+K{e}^{0} \\ 78 & =12+K \\ K & =66\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=12+66{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $12$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${58}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(12)=58,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}58 & =12+66{e}^{-12k} \\ 46 & =66{e}^{-12k} \\ \frac{23}{33} & ={e}^{-12k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{23}{33}\right) & =-12k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{23}{33}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the thermometer reads ${28}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =28 \\ 12+66{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =28 \\ 66{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =16 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{8}{33} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{8}{33}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{8}{33}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the thermometer will read ${28}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{8}{33}\right)}{-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{23}{33}\right)}≈47\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={12}^{∘}\text{F},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-12).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-12| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-12 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-12 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-12 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =12+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${81}^{∘}F.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=81,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}81 & =12+K{e}^{0} \\ 81 & =12+K \\ K & =69\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=12+69{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $12$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${58}^{∘}F.$ So, applying the condition $T(12)=58,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}58 & =12+69{e}^{-12k} \\ 46 & =69{e}^{-12k} \\ \frac{46}{69} & ={e}^{-12k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{46}{69}\right) & =-12k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{46}{69}\right)\end{aligned}

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: A heated metal body cools in a room at ${12}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Its temperature is ${83}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $2$ minutes and ${62}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $7$ minutes. The temperature $T(t)$, in degrees Celsius, obeys Newton's law of cooling, with $t$ measured in minutes since cooling began. To the nearest minute, how long after cooling began does the body reach ${26}^{∘}\text{C}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-12),\qquad k>0.
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-12| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-12>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-12 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-12 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-12 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =12+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

Apply the two observed conditions $T(2)=83$ and $T(7)=62$:

$$
\begin{aligned}83 & =12+Ke^{-2k} \\ 71 & =Ke^{-2k} \\ 62 & =12+Ke^{-7k} \\ 50 & =Ke^{-7k}\end{aligned}
$$

Divide the excess temperatures to eliminate $K$, then take natural logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{50}{71} & =\frac{Ke^{-7k}}{Ke^{-2k}} \\ \frac{50}{71} & =e^{-5k} \\ \ln\left(\frac{50}{71}\right) & =-5k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute this rate into $T(2)=83$ to determine the constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}71 & =Ke^{-2\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\right)} \\ K & =71e^{2\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\right)} \\ K & =71\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^{\frac{2}{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=12+71\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^{\frac{2}{5}}e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\right)t}.
$$

Substituting the two observation times confirms the model:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(2) & =12+(71\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^{\frac{2}{5}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\right)\cdot 2}=83 \\ T(7) & =12+(71\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^{\frac{2}{5}})e^{-\left(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}\right)\cdot 7}=62\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the body reaches ${26}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =26 \\ 12+Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =26 \\ Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =14 \\ e^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{14}{K} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\ln\left(\frac{14}{K}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{14}{K}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the values of $K$ and $k$ to obtain the time measured since cooling began:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{50}{71} \right)}}{5}}\ln\left(\frac{14}{71\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^{\frac{2}{5}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =2+5\frac{\ln\left(\frac{14}{71}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{50}{71}\right)}≈25\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{x+2y}{x}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{x+2(vx)}{x} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=1+2v \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=1+v \\ \frac{1}{1+v}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{1}{1+v}\,\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \ln|v+1|&=\ln|x|+C_1 \\ |v+1|&=e^{C_1}|x| \\ v+1&=Cx \\ v&=Cx-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x}&=Cx-1 \\ y&=Cx^2-x\end{aligned}
$$

The signed constant $C$ absorbs $e^{C_1}$. Division by $v+1$ excluded $v=-1$; restoring it permits $C=0$, giving $y=-x$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$.

question.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{x^3+y^3}{xy^2}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{x^3+(vx)^3}{x(vx)^2} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{1+v^3}{v^2}=\frac{1}{v^2}+v \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{v^2} \\ v^2\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v^2\,\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{v^3}{3}&=\ln|x|+C_1 \\ v^3&=3\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^3&=3\ln|x|+C \\ y^3&=x^3(3\ln|x|+C) \\ y&=x\sqrt[3]{3\ln|x|+C}\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=3C_1$ and the cube root is real. Restrict the solution to intervals where $y\ne0$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{y^3+xy^2+x^2y+x^3}{xy^2+x^2y}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a homogeneous equation because all terms in the numerator and denominator have degree 3 (cubic).

With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{(vx)^3+x(vx)^2+x^2(vx)+x^3}{x(vx)^2+x^2(vx)} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{v^3+v^2+v+1}{v^2+v} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{v^3+v^2+v+1}{v^2+v}-v \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{(v+1)}{v(v+1)}=\frac{1}{v} \\ v\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\,\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{v^2}{2}&=\ln|x|+C_1 \\ v^2&=2\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y^2}{x^2}&=2\ln|x|+C \\ y^2&=x^2(2\ln|x|+C)\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=2C_1$. The original denominator excludes $v=0$ and $v=-1$, so the cancellation is valid only on those intervals.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$, $y\ne0$, and $y\ne-x$.

\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{yx}{y^2+x^2}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{(vx)x}{(vx)^2+x^2} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{v}{v^2+1} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{v}{v^2+1}-v=-\frac{v^3}{v^2+1} \\ \frac{v^2+1}{v^3}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{v^2+1}{v^3}\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int\left(\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{v^3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ \ln|v|-\frac{1}{2v^2}&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ 2\ln|v|-\frac{1}{v^2}&=-2\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\ln\left|\frac{y}{x}\right|-\frac{x^2}{y^2}&=-2\ln|x|+C \\ 2\ln\left|\frac{y}{x}\right|+2\ln|x|-\frac{x^2}{y^2}&=C \\ 2\ln|y|-\frac{x^2}{y^2}&=C\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=2C_1$. The constant solution $y=0$ was excluded by the question; division by $v$ is therefore valid.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

knowledge_point.title: Solving a Homogeneous Differential Equation

question.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{x+y}{x}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{x+(vx)}{x} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=1+v \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=1 \\ \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ v&=\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x}&=\ln|x|+C \\ y&=x\ln|x|+Cx\end{aligned}
$$



The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$.

knowledge_point.title: Solving a Homogeneous Differential Equation

question.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{y}{x}\left(\ln\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+1\right)
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{vx}{x}\left(\ln\left(\frac{vx}{x}\right)+1\right) \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=v(\ln v+1) \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=v\ln v \\ \frac{1}{v\ln v}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{1}{v\ln v}\,\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ u&=\ln v,\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}v}=\frac{1}{v} \\ \int\frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u&=\ln|x|+C \\ \ln|\ln v|&=\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\ln\left|\ln\frac{y}{x}\right|&=\ln|x|+C \\ \left|\ln\frac{y}{x}\right|&=e^C|x|^{1} \\ \ln\frac{y}{x}&=Kx \\ \frac{y}{x}&=e^{Kx} \\ y&=xe^{Kx}\end{aligned}
$$

The signed constant $K$ absorbs $e^C$ and the fixed sign of $x$ on the interval. The division by $\ln v$ excluded $v=1$; restoring it allows $K=0$, giving $y=x$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y/x>0$.

knowledge_point.title: Solving a Homogeneous Differential Equation

question.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{x^2+3y^2}{2xy}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{1x^2+3(vx)^2}{2x(vx)} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{1+3v^2}{2v} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1+v^2}{2v} \\ \frac{2v}{1+v^2}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{2v}{1+v^2}\,\mathrm{d}v&=\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \ln(1+v^2)&=\ln|x|+C_1 \\ 1+v^2&=Kx \\ v^2&=Kx-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y^2}{x^2}&=Kx-1 \\ y^2&=Kx^3-x^2\end{aligned}
$$

Here $K$ absorbs the exponential constant and the sign of $x$ on the interval. Use real branches where the original equation is defined.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

knowledge_point.title: Solving a Homogeneous Differential Equation

question.:question/problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation. Consider the solutions with $y\ne0$.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{y^3}{xy^2+x^3}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{(vx)^3}{x(vx)^2+x^3} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{v^3}{v^2+1} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{v^3}{v^2+1}-v=-\frac{v}{v^2+1} \\ \frac{v^2+1}{v}\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int\frac{v^2+1}{v}\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int\left(v+\frac{1}{v}\right)\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ \frac{v^2}{2}+\ln|v|&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ v^2+\ln(v^2)&=-\ln(x^2)+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y^2}{x^2}+\ln\left(\frac{y^2}{x^2}\right)&=-\ln(x^2)+C \\ \frac{y^2}{x^2}+\ln(y^2)-\ln(x^2)&=-\ln(x^2)+C \\ \frac{y^2}{x^2}+\ln(y^2)&=C \\ \frac{y^2}{x^2}&=C-\ln(y^2) \\ \frac{y^2}{C-\ln(y^2)}&=x^2\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=2C_1$. The constant solution $y=0$ was excluded by the question. On the nonzero solution, the final denominator equals $y^2/x^2>0$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

knowledge_point.title: Solving a Homogeneous Differential Equation

question.:question/problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation.

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{y^2-x^2}{xy}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a homogeneous equation because all terms in the numerator and denominator have degree 2 (quadratic).

With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x) \\ &=x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{(vx)^2-x^2}{x(vx)} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}+v&=\frac{v^2-1}{v} \\ x\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{v^2-1}{v}-v=-\frac{1}{v} \\ v\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}&=-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\,\mathrm{d}v&=-\int\frac{1}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{v^2}{2}&=-\ln|x|+C_1 \\ v^2&=-2\ln|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y^2}{x^2}&=-2\ln|x|+C \\ \frac{y^2}{x^2}&=-\ln(x^2)+C \\ y^2&=-x^2\ln(x^2)+Cx^2\end{aligned}
$$

Here $C=2C_1$; use $2\ln|x|=\ln(x^2)$.

The solution is used on intervals where $x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$.

knowledge_point.title: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=\frac{2 x - 11}{y}.$ Work on intervals where $y\ne 0$ and the radicand is positive.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =\frac{2 x - 11}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =2 x - 11\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 2 x - 11\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2} & =x + \left(x - 6\right)^{2} - 6+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
\frac{y^{2}}{2}=x + \left(x - 6\right)^{2} - 6+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ Solving for $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y^2 & =2 x + 2 \left(x - 6\right)^{2} - 12+2C \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{2 x + 2 \left(x - 6\right)^{2} - 12+2C} \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{2 x + 2 \left(x - 6\right)^{2} - 12+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=2C$ is an arbitrary real constant.

knowledge_point.title: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=2 y^{2} + 2.$ Work on intervals avoiding tangent poles.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =2 y^{2} + 2 \\ \frac{1}{y^{2} + 1}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 2\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \arctan{\left(y \right)} & =2 x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
\arctan{\left(y \right)}=2 x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ Solving for $y$ gives

$$
y=\tan{\left(C + 2 x \right)}.
$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant.

knowledge_point.title: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=\frac{4 \left(x - 3\right)^{3}}{y}.$ Assume $x-3>0.$ Take both sign branches on intervals where the radicand is positive and $y\ne 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =\frac{4 \left(x - 3\right)^{3}}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =4 \left(x - 3\right)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\int 4 \left(x - 3\right)^{3}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int y\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 4 \left(x - 3\right)^{3}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2} & =\left(x - 3\right)^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{y^{2}}{2}=\left(x - 3\right)^{4}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y^2 & =2 \left(x - 3\right)^{4}+2C \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{2 \left(x - 3\right)^{4}+2C} \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{2 \left(x - 3\right)^{4}+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=2C$ is an arbitrary real constant. Use either sign consistently on each interval where the radicand is positive.

knowledge_point.title: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=\left(12 x - 72\right)\sqrt[3]{y^2}.$ Work on intervals where $y\ne 0$; cube roots are real.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =\left(12 x - 72\right)\sqrt[3]{y^2} \\ \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{y^2}}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =4 x - 24\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{y^2}}\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int 4 x - 24\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \sqrt[3]{y} & =2 \left(x - 6\right)^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
\sqrt[3]{y}=2 \left(x - 6\right)^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ Solving for $y$ gives

$$
y=\left(C + 2 \left(x - 6\right)^{2}\right)^{3}.
$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant.

knowledge_point.title: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=e^{5 x - y}.$ Work on intervals where the logarithm argument is positive.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =e^{5 x - y} \\ e^{y}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =e^{5 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int e^{y}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\int e^{5 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int e^{y}\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int e^{5 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ e^{y} & =\frac{e^{5 x}}{5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
e^{y}=\frac{e^{5 x}}{5}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\ln{\left(C + \frac{e^{5 x}}{5} \right)}.
$$

The logarithm argument must be positive on the solution interval; $C$ is an arbitrary real constant.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{1-{(x+6)}^{2}}}$ for $y\ne 0$ and $|(x+6)|<1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{\sqrt{1-{(x+6)}^{2}}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{\sqrt{1-{(x+6)}^{2}}} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(x+6)}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(x+6)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(x+6)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(x+6)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x+6)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x+6)+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x+6)+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x+6)+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x+6)}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x+6)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x+6)}.
$$

Here $K$ is arbitrary and nonzero.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+6)$ for $y\ne 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+6) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+6) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x+6)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x+6)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x+6)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+6)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+6)+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+6)+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+6)+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+6)}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+6)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

y=K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+6)}.
$$

Here $K$ is arbitrary and nonzero.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}={(x+6)}^{2}y$ for $y\ne 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={(x+6)}^{2}y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={(x+6)}^{2}y \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={(x+6)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$

$$

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\frac{1}{3}\,{(x+6)}^{3}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{(x+6)}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{(x+6)}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{(x+6)}^{3}/3}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{{(x+6)}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{{(x+6)}^{3}/3}.
$$

Here $K$ is arbitrary and nonzero.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x+6)}$ for $y\ne 0$ and $-\frac{\pi }{2}<(x+6)<\frac{\pi }{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x+6)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x+6)} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡(x+6)} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={sec}^{2}⁡(x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(x+6)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(x+6)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(x+6)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+6)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{tan}⁡(x+6)+C.
$$

Use a local interval on which the integrated, separated equation holds on its positive branch.
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}{y}^{′} & =8 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 8\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y & =\int 8\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}y & =\int 8{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ 2{y}^{1/2} & =\frac{16}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
2{y}^{1/2}=\frac{16}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{1/2} & =\frac{16}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C \\ {y}^{1/2} & =\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3/2}+\frac{C}{2} \\ y & ={(\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3/2}+\frac{C}{2})}^{2} \\ y & ={(\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3/2}+K)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\frac{C}{2}.$

The displayed family is valid locally where $K + \frac{8 x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}>0.$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\big|_{x=0} & =(4)\cdot {5}^{4(0)-1}\ln(5) \\ & =4\cdot {5}^{-1}\ln(5) \\ & =\frac{4 \ln{\left(5 \right)}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=x-3.$ Then $f=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$

and

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-3}}+9x^{2}.

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={5}^{x-4y}
$$

Work on an open domain where all displayed expressions are defined and the dependent-variable factor is nonzero. Choose an equivalent equation in the form $A(y)\, \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=B(x)$, with a multiplier depending only on $y$ and a right-hand side depending only on $x$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A differential equation is *separable* if it can be written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x)g(y).
$$

If an equation is separable, we say that the variables are *separated* when it is written in the form

$$
\frac{1}{g(y)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=h(x).
$$

Notice that our differential equation is separable since it can be written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={5}^{x}\cdot {5}^{-4y}
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
{5}^{4y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={5}^{x}\,.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Separate the variables in the following differential equation: 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4x+x{y}^{4}+16+4{y}^{4}}{4x}
$$

Work on an open domain where all displayed expressions are defined and the dependent-variable factor is nonzero. Choose an equivalent equation in the form $A(y)\, \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=B(x)$, with a multiplier depending only on $y$ and a right-hand side depending only on $x$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Expose the independent-variable and dependent-variable factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4x+x{y}^{4}+16+4{y}^{4}}{4x} \\ & =\frac{x(4+{y}^{4})+4(4+{y}^{4})}{4x} \\ & =\frac{(x+4)(4+{y}^{4})}{4x} \\ & =\frac{x+4}{4x}\cdot (4+{y}^{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply both sides by the reciprocal of the dependent-variable factor. On the stated domain, this gives

$$
\frac{1}{4+{y}^{4}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x+4}{4x}.
$$

The derivative multiplier depends only on $y$ and the right-hand side only on $x$.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2 \sqrt{1 - \left(y - 5\right)^{2}}$ for $\,|\left(y-5\right)|<1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 \sqrt{1 - \left(y - 5\right)^{2}} \\ \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \left(y - 5\right)^{2}}}\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \left(y - 5\right)^{2}}}\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \left(y - 5\right)^{2}}}\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (2)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \left(y - 5\right)^{2}}}\right)\,\text{d}y & =\int (2)\,\text{d}x \\ \arcsin{\left(y - 5 \right)} & =2 x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\arcsin{\left(y - 5 \right)}=2 x+C.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+e^{- y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2 x e^{- y} - 2 e^{2 x - y}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Collect the derivative terms, then multiply both sides by $e^y$ to separate the variables.

$$
\begin{aligned}(1 + e^{- y})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 x e^{- y} - 2 e^{2 x - y} \\ (e^{y} + 1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2 x - 2 e^{2 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate both sides term by term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (e^{y} + 1)\,\text{d}y & =\int (2 x - 2 e^{2 x})\,\text{d}x \\ y + e^{y} & =x^{2} - e^{2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution in implicit form is

$$
y + e^{y}=x^{2} - e^{2 x}+C.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given that $f(x)=\left(4 x - 3\right)^{3}$, find $f^{\prime}(x).$

Use the decomposition $g(x)=4 x - 3$ and $F(u)=u^{3}$, so $f(x)=F(g(x))$. Recall that $f^{\prime}(x)=F^{\prime}(g(x))g^{\prime}(x)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $g(x)=4 x - 3$ and $F(g)=g^{3}$, so $f(x)=F(g(x))$.

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} F^{\prime}(g)&=3 g^{2}, \\ g^{\prime}(x)&=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule,

$$
\begin{aligned} f^{\prime}(x)&=F^{\prime}(g(x))\cdot g^{\prime}(x) \\ &=\left(3 \left(4 x - 3\right)^{2}\right)\cdot\left(4\right) \\ &=12 \left(4 x - 3\right)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
